newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan earthquake swarm may mean volcanic activity.
newsitem.headline: Japan earthquake swarm may mean volcanic activity.

text.p: More than 2,500 small earthquakes have jolted a Japanese seaside and spa resort south of Tokyo over the past 48 hours, including two tremors which may signal volcanic activity, the Meteorological Agency said on Tuesday.
Three people were slightly injured by falling objects but there were no reports of major damage in the series of tremors, police said.

The agency said the earthquake swarm started shaking Ito, 120 km (75 miles) southwest of Tokyo, on Monday and the number of tremors had reached 2,531 by mid-afternoon on Tuesday. Of the total, 86 were strong enough to be felt, it said.
The strongest so far measured 5.6 on the Richter scale and came at 12.57 p.m. (0357 GMT) on Tuesday and shook Tokyo as well as the Ito area.
The agency also reported two "low-frequency earthquakes", which could indicate undersea volcanic activity, on Tuesday morning.
"Volcanic activity is not always the cause of these low-frequency tremors, but they did occur just before a submarine volcano erupted there in 1989," an agency seismologist said.
A small underwater eruption off Ito in 1989 caused a tremor measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale but no damage.
The agency said it dispatched a specialist team of seismologists and volcanologists to the region to step up monitoring activity.
One of the stronger tremors late on Monday triggered a small landslide which destroyed a warehouse. A dozen water and gas mains were severed, police said.
Several local residents were evacuated to a city hall, police said. Ito, a city of 72,000 people, is famous for hot springs and seafood.
Local rail authorities said they took precautionary measures to halt rail services on Tuesday.

The focal points of the latest earthquake swarm ranged in depth from a few hundred metres (yards) to about 10 km (six miles) under the surface of the sea, the agency said. Shallow focal points could indicate renewed volcanic activity in the area, agency officials said.
Last October, Ito was shaken by another earthquake swarm of more than 5,000 tremors, only a few of which could be felt. There was no damage.
